newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-US Nov payrolls -fewer jobs, higher wages.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-US Nov payrolls -fewer jobs, higher wages.

text.p: The U.S. economy probably generated fewer jobs in November than it did in October, Wall Street economists said.
But those Americans who had a job most likely made more money for their hours at work, which could be seen as a sign of economic strength, they added.
"In October you saw a sharp drop in hours worked plus flat wages, which gave you a weakened report," said Joseph Carson, chief fixed-income economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"In November, tax receipts show a strong rebound, which implies a pretty good gain in wages and salary income for the month," Carson added.

A recent Reuters survey showed U.S. experts are expecting, on average, a small drop in November non-farm payrolls to 179,000 jobs against 210,000 in October, while the joblessness rate is seen steady at 5.2 percent.
The U.S. Labor Department is scheduled to release the November payrolls report in Washington on Friday at 0830 EST / 1330 GMT.
Average hourly earnings earnings, however, is expected to post a 0.4 percent rise against a flat index last month. The average workweek is seen up at 34.4 hours against 34.3 hours.

"I think that what's happening is basically that the economy is probably a little bit stronger than the Gross Domestic Product suggests," said William Dudley, senior economist at Goldman Sachs & Co. Inc.
"There seems to be a disparity between what's happening in the income side of the account versus what's happening in the GDP side of the account," he added.
The latest GDP report showed the economy slowed in the third quarter to a 2.2 percent growth rate from a breakneck 4.7 percent pace in the second quarter.
Analysts said most of the strength in the report is expected to stem from the service sector, although the manufacturing labor market is also expected to show life.
"I think you'll see manufacturing (sector) a little bit less negative than it has been. But the service sector is where you're going to see the bulk of the gain," Goldman's Dudley said.

Analysts said the end of the General Motors strike, which started in Canada but ended up forcing some U.S. plants to shut down, was also likely to provide a clearer picture of employment levels in the manufacturing sector.
"A lot of the softness that we've seen on the manufacturing side was really in the auto sector," said William Griggs, managing director at consulting firm Griggs and Santow Inc.
"Now I think that what comes through (in November) is the undistorted numbers," Griggs added.
If the report comes in as expected, economists said it will reinforce the idea that the fourth quarter of the year will be fairly stronger than the weak third quarter.
Economists said firm hourly earnings and a payroll gain between 180,000 and 200,000 is likely to bring GDP growth to somewhere between 2.5 and 3.0 percent in the fourth quarter.

Although the economy is believed to have regained part of its underlying strength after a weak third quarter, most economists do not believe the November employment report will prompt the Federal Reserve to change monetary policy.
"I think the Fed is firmly locked on hold for the time being," Dudley said. "I think it will be several months before the Fed begin to seriously contemplate adjustments to (monetary) policy."
The Fed last changed monetary policy in January, when it trimmed its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent.
